executive_summary.tagline: Empowering farmers market vendors with simple tools to manage inventory, accept payments, and grow their business.
executive_summary.problem_statement: Farmers market vendors struggle with inefficient manual inventory tracking, limited payment options (especially SNAP/EBT), and reconciliation of cash and digital transactions, leading to lost sales, wasted time, and exclusion of low-income customers.
executive_summary.solution_overview: MarketMate is a mobile-first platform that provides farmers market vendors with intuitive inventory management, integrated payment processing (including SNAP/EBT), sales tracking, and customer management tools, all designed to streamline operations and increase revenue.
executive_summary.value_proposition: MarketMate offers an affordable, easy-to-use solution tailored to the unique needs of farmers market vendors, enabling them to accept more payment types, reduce administrative overhead, and focus on building relationships with their customers. Unlike Square's generic POS system, MarketMate specializes in inventory management for perishables and SNAP/EBT acceptance.
target_users: Small farmers market vendors in California: Family-owned farms and independent artisans with limited tech experience and a need for simple, affordable solutions.
Farmers market organizations: Associations seeking to modernize their markets and attract a wider customer base by facilitating SNAP/EBT acceptance.
executive_summary.target_market_size: TAM: $10B (10% of farm direct sales). SAM: $1B (California farmers market vendors). SOM: $10M (San Francisco Bay Area farmers market vendors). These estimates are based on industry reports on direct farm sales and the proportion of sales occurring at farmers markets.
key_differentiators: SNAP/EBT Integration: Unlike Square, MarketMate offers seamless SNAP/EBT processing, expanding vendors' customer base and aligning with community needs.
Perishable Inventory Management: MarketMate is optimized for the unique challenges of tracking perishable goods, reducing waste and maximizing sales, a feature lacking in general-purpose POS systems.
Community Focus: MarketMate builds strong relationships with farmers market associations to provide tailored solutions and support, differentiating from competitors with a broader market focus.
executive_summary.competitive_landscape: The market is dominated by general-purpose POS systems like Square, which offer basic features but lack specialized functionality for farmers markets. MarketMate differentiates by focusing on niche needs like SNAP/EBT and perishable inventory, creating a competitive advantage in this underserved segment.
executive_summary.revenue_model: Freemium model with a 'Starter' plan (basic features, transaction fees) and a 'Pro' subscription plan (unlimited features, lower transaction fees, SNAP/EBT processing).
executive_summary.financial_projections: Year 1: $413,000 revenue. Year 3: $2.5M revenue, assuming successful expansion and adoption of the Pro plan.
top_risks: Competition from established POS systems: Mitigate by focusing on niche features, building strong relationships with farmers market associations, and rapid product iteration based on user feedback.
Technology integration issues: Mitigate by thorough testing, robust API design, and phased rollout of new features.
Low adoption rate due to tech hesitance: Mitigate by providing excellent customer support, intuitive user interface, and hands-on training at farmers markets.
executive_summary.regulatory_summary: Compliance with CCPA (California Consumer Privacy Act) and PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) is required. Estimated compliance timeline: 3-6 months. Estimated compliance cost: $10,000 - $30,000.
executive_summary.gtm_strategy: Direct sales and partnerships with farmers market associations, starting with a beachhead market in the San Francisco Bay Area.
key_milestones: Launch beta program in SF Bay Area (3 months)
Secure partnerships with 3+ farmers market associations (6 months)
Expand to Los Angeles and San Diego (12 months)
success_metrics: Number of paying customers: Target 100 in the first 9 months.
Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR): Target $5,000 MRR by month 12.
Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC): Maintain CAC below $500 in the first year.
Customer Churn Rate: Maintain churn rate below 5% per month.
Customer Satisfaction (CSAT) Score: Achieve a CSAT score of 4.5 out of 5.

technical_architecture.architecture_style: Microservices. This architecture is chosen to allow for independent scaling and deployment of different functionalities, such as inventory management, payment processing, and reporting. This also allows for technology diversity, enabling us to use the best tool for each specific job. This approach will aid in easier maintenance and faster development cycles, especially as the team grows. While a monolith might be simpler to start, the microservices architecture provides the necessary flexibility and resilience for long-term growth.
technical_architecture.architecture_diagram_description: The system architecture is based on a microservices design. The mobile app interacts with the API Gateway, which routes requests to the appropriate microservice. The core microservices include Inventory Management, Sales Management, Payment Processing, and Reporting. Each microservice has its own database. Redis is used for caching frequently accessed data. Background tasks, such as generating reports and sending notifications, are handled by a message queue (RabbitMQ). External services, like the SNAP/EBT processor, are integrated through APIs.

technical_architecture.data_storage: PostgreSQL is the primary data store for all microservices due to its reliability and ACID properties. Read replicas will be used for the reporting service to offload read traffic from the primary database. Data will be partitioned based on vendor ID to improve query performance. Regular backups will be performed and stored offsite. Data retention policies will be implemented to comply with data privacy regulations.
technical_architecture.security_architecture: Authentication will be handled using JWT (JSON Web Tokens) issued by Auth0. Authorization will be based on RBAC (Role-Based Access Control), with different roles for vendors, admins, and customers. Data will be encrypted at rest using AES-256 encryption and in transit using HTTPS. API security measures include rate limiting, input validation, and protection against common web vulnerabilities. Compliance with PCI DSS will be ensured for payment processing.
technical_architecture.scalability_approach: Horizontal scaling will be used for all microservices, with auto-scaling triggered based on CPU utilization and request latency. The database will be scaled using read replicas and sharding. Redis will be used for caching frequently accessed data to reduce database load. A CDN will be used to serve static assets.
technical_architecture.deployment_strategy: A multi-environment structure will be used, with separate environments for development, staging, and production. Docker containers will be used for packaging and deploying the microservices. Kubernetes will be used for orchestration and management of the containers. Blue-green deployments will be used for zero-downtime deployments. Rollback procedures will be in place to quickly revert to a previous version in case of issues.

risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Reduce operating expenses, seek additional investment, or consider a strategic acquisition.

risk_matrix.name: Lack of Team Expertise
risk_matrix.description: Inexperience in agriculture tech or payment processing could lead to poor decisions.
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Hire experienced personnel, provide training, and establish mentorship programs.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Outsource critical functions, bring in external consultants.

risk_matrix.name: Regulatory Changes
risk_matrix.description: Changes in regulations regarding EBT or data privacy could require costly updates.
triggers: New laws or regulations affecting payment processing or data privacy
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Stay informed about regulatory changes, engage with industry groups, and build compliance into the product from the start.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Adapt the product to comply with new regulations, seek legal counsel.

risk_matrix.name: Seasonality
risk_matrix.description: Farmers markets are often seasonal, leading to fluctuating revenue.
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Offer features that are useful year-round (e.g., online ordering, inventory management for storage), target markets with longer seasons.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Reduce operating expenses during the off-season, focus on customer retention.

risk_matrix.name: Data Security Breach
risk_matrix.description: Compromised customer data could lead to financial losses and reputational damage.
early_warning_signs: Reports of data breaches in similar companies
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Implement robust security measures, conduct regular security audits, and train employees on security best practices.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Incident response plan, notify affected customers, and cooperate with law enforcement.

risk_matrix.name: Pricing Model Not Viable
risk_matrix.description: The chosen pricing structure may not attract enough customers or generate sufficient revenue.
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Conduct market research to determine optimal pricing, offer flexible pricing options, and monitor competitor pricing.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Adjust pricing model, offer discounts or promotions.

risk_matrix.name: Scalability Issues
risk_matrix.description: The app may not be able to handle a large number of users or transactions.
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Implement scalable infrastructure, optimize code, and conduct load testing.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Scale up server capacity, implement caching mechanisms.

risk_matrix.name: Dependence on Farmers Market Associations
risk_matrix.description: Reliance on partnerships with farmers market associations can be risky if these relationships sour.
triggers: Negative publicity from farmers market associations
Competition from other vendors endorsed by the associations
early_warning_signs: Decreased communication with farmers market associations
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Diversify partnerships, build strong relationships with individual vendors, and offer incentives for referrals.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Seek alternative distribution channels, focus on direct marketing to vendors.

risk_matrix.name: Low Technology Adoption by Target Users
risk_matrix.description: Farmers may be resistant to using new technology.
early_warning_signs: High customer support tickets related to app functionality
Lack of engagement with training materials
risk_matrix.mitigation_strategy: Focus on simplicity and ease of use, provide extensive training and support, and offer incentives for adoption.
risk_matrix.contingency_plan: Simplify the app even further, offer personalized onboarding support.

top_3_risks.name: Technology Integration Issues
top_3_risks.why_critical: Failed payment integrations directly impact revenue and customer trust.
top_3_risks.immediate_action: Prioritize robust testing and monitoring of payment integrations.

top_3_risks.name: Seasonality
top_3_risks.why_critical: Fluctuating revenue makes financial planning difficult and may lead to cash flow problems.
top_3_risks.immediate_action: Develop strategies to generate revenue during the off-season.

top_3_risks.name: Competition from Existing POS Systems
top_3_risks.why_critical: Established players have a head start and may quickly replicate key features.
top_3_risks.immediate_action: Aggressively market unique value proposition and build strong customer relationships.

risk_interdependencies.cascade_effect: Technical issues can lead to security breaches and scalability problems, impacting user experience and trust.
Insufficient funding can be exacerbated by seasonality and a non-viable pricing model, leading to project failure.

risk_appetite_recommendation.rationale: The product is targeting a relatively conservative market (farmers), and the business model relies on building trust and long-term relationships. A moderate risk appetite allows for calculated risks with a focus on stability and sustainability.
conditions_for_go: Successful completion of payment integration testing
Secure partnerships with at least three farmers market associations
Adequate funding secured for the first year of operations

key_risk_indicators.action_if_exceeded: Investigate and resolve payment integration issues immediately. Communicate with affected customers.
Analyze churn data to identify the causes and implement retention strategies.
Evaluate the effectiveness of marketing campaigns and optimize marketing spend.

monitoring_plan.escalation_process: Risks exceeding the threshold will be escalated to the executive team for review and action.

prototype.primary_persona: Maria Rodriguez — Market Vendor & Farm Manager
prototype.key_user_story: As a vendor preparing for market day, Maria wants to quickly add a new seasonal product to her digital inventory so she can accurately track its stock and sales from the start.
prototype.story_summary: The prototype follows Maria, a market vendor, as she logs in and sees a low stock alert for her apples. This prompts her to add a new seasonal item, 'Golden Zucchini', via a simple form. The 'aha moment' occurs when she sees the instant confirmation, realizing how effortlessly she can manage her digital inventory, saving time and preventing tracking errors.
prototype.state_management_notes: Uses React's `useState` hook for all state management. `currentScreen` controls which view is displayed, enabling navigation. `inventory` holds the list of products, allowing for dynamic updates like adding a new item. `newProduct` manages the state of the controlled form components for adding a new product.
interactivity_notes: Clickable sidebar navigation items that update the `currentScreen` state to render different views.
The 'Add New Product' button on the inventory screen navigates the user to a dedicated form.
A fully interactive 'Add Product' form with controlled inputs that update state on change.
Form submission buttons trigger state changes, update the mock data, and navigate to a confirmation screen.
prototype.demo_scenario:
1. Start on the 'Inventory' screen. Point out the professional, clean layout. Highlight the 'Low Stock Alert' for 'Honeycrisp Apples' and say, 'This is what catches Maria's eye. She realizes she needs to prep her new produce for the market.'
2. Click the 'Add New Product' button. 'To solve this, Maria can quickly add her new seasonal item.'
3. On the 'Add Product Form', briefly show how easy it is to fill out the details for 'Golden Zucchini'. The form is pre-filled to save time. Say, 'The form is simple and tailored to her needs—no complex fields.'
4. Click the 'Save Product' button. 'With one click...'
5. Land on the 'Product Added!' confirmation screen. '...the product is in her system. This is the aha moment. In under 30 seconds, her inventory is updated, accurate, and ready for market day—a task that used to involve messy spreadsheets.'
6. Click 'Return to Inventory' to show the newly added 'Golden Zucchini' at the top of the list.
prototype.design_notes: The design uses a professional and trustworthy color palette (navy, forest green) appropriate for a B2B/retail tool, but with a clean, approachable feel to not intimidate the 'Tech-Hesitant Traditionalist' persona. Generous whitespace, clear typography hierarchy, and familiar icons (Lucide) create an intuitive user experience. Interactive elements have clear hover and active states to provide immediate feedback. The bar chart on the sales screen is intentionally simple, made of divs to be easily understood at a glance without overwhelming the user with complex chart libraries.

views.tailored_summary:
This initiative targets a well-defined, underserved market of farmers market vendors with clear monetization potential. The proposed business model utilizes a dual revenue stream—a freemium tier to drive adoption and a premium subscription ('Pro Plan') for high-value features, supplemented by transaction fees. Initial projections indicate the Pro Plan will contribute 60% of revenue, demonstrating a strong path to profitability.

While the initial cost structure is lean, focusing on a core product and engineering team, it's designed for capital efficiency. Key financial hypotheses, such as the blended Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) of $500 and a Lifetime Value (LTV) of $2500, present a healthy 5:1 LTV:CAC ratio. The primary financial risks are market competition and the accuracy of these early-stage assumptions, which our go-to-market strategy aims to validate quickly and cost-effectively within the initial beachhead market.
key_questions_answered: What is the proposed revenue model and its projected contribution mix?
What is the initial cost structure and burn rate?
What are the key unit economics (LTV, CAC) and the underlying assumptions?
What are the primary financial risks and mitigation strategies?

anticipated_objections.objection: The revenue and LTV projections are based on hypotheses and seem optimistic for a new entrant.
anticipated_objections.response: This is acknowledged. The projections are based on the serviceable market size and the value provided by unique features like SNAP/EBT processing. The model's primary purpose is to establish initial viability. We will validate these assumptions with real-world data from our beachhead market launch and adjust accordingly.

anticipated_objections.objection: A blended CAC of $500 is high. Can we acquire customers more profitably?
anticipated_objections.response: The initial blended CAC is conservative, reflecting higher-cost direct sales and partnership efforts needed to enter the market. As we scale, we expect CAC to decrease significantly by optimizing lower-cost channels like content marketing and online advertising, which have a projected CAC as low as $25.

anticipated_objections.objection: The freemium 'Starter Plan' could lead to high support costs with low revenue conversion.
anticipated_objections.response: The Starter Plan is a strategic acquisition tool designed to lower the adoption barrier for our tech-hesitant persona. Its feature set is limited to encourage upgrades. We will monitor the conversion rate from Starter to Pro closely as a key performance indicator and adjust the offering if the unit economics prove unfavorable.

views.decision_recommendation: Recommend proceeding with seed funding to validate the core financial model in the San Francisco Bay Area market. Mandate stringent monthly reviews of CAC, LTV, and conversion metrics to ensure the project remains on a path to profitability.

views.tailored_summary:
This project involves handling sensitive vendor and customer data, including personal information and payment details, placing data security and regulatory compliance at the forefront. The initial assessment correctly identifies the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) as an applicable regulation due to our target market. The proposed technical architecture, while offering scalability, introduces a broader attack surface via its microservices design that will require robust security controls from the outset.

The most significant risk identified is the handling of payment data. While not explicitly stated, achieving PCI DSS compliance is non-negotiable. The strategy should be to de-scope our environment by integrating with a certified third-party payment processor. This will transfer a significant portion of the compliance burden, but not eliminate our responsibility to secure the application and protect customer PII.
key_questions_answered: What are the applicable data privacy regulations and our plan to comply?
How will we secure sensitive payment information?
What are the security implications of the proposed microservices architecture?
What are the top security and compliance risks identified?

anticipated_objections.objection: The plan completely omits PCI DSS, which is a critical compliance requirement for handling card payments.
anticipated_objections.response: This is a correct and critical observation. The implicit strategy is to integrate with a Level 1 PCI-compliant payment gateway (e.g., Stripe, Braintree), which would place the burden of storing and transmitting cardholder data on them. This must be made an explicit requirement, and our architecture must ensure sensitive card data never touches our servers.

anticipated_objections.objection: Microservices increase the attack surface and operational complexity from a security perspective.
anticipated_objections.response: While the attack surface is larger, this architecture allows for better isolation and containment. We can apply specific, stringent security policies to critical services like payments and authentication, rather than a single policy for a monolith. This requires a strong focus on API security, service-to-service authentication, and centralized logging from day one.

anticipated_objections.objection: The initial personnel budget has no allocation for a dedicated security role.
anticipated_objections.response: You are correct. For the MVP phase, security responsibilities will be embedded within the engineering team, following secure coding practices. However, we must budget for third-party penetration testing before launch and allocate funding for a dedicated security hire or consultant as we scale post-launch and our data footprint grows.

views.decision_recommendation: Recommend conditional approval, contingent on the development of a formal security and compliance roadmap. This roadmap must explicitly detail the PCI DSS compliance strategy via a third-party processor, outline a threat model for the MVP, and budget for a pre-launch security audit.

views.tailored_summary:
The proposal outlines a modern technical approach using a microservices architecture built on Node.js and React Native. The primary justification for microservices is long-term scalability and development velocity by enabling independent deployment of key domains like inventory, payments, and reporting. This choice, while ambitious for an initial product, is defensible given the distinct nature of these business capabilities.

The technology stack is pragmatic, leveraging well-supported, mainstream technologies like React Native for cross-platform mobile development and a standard Node.js backend. This reduces hiring friction and development time. The key architectural risk is the operational overhead of microservices for a small team. The success of this architecture will depend heavily on robust CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure-as-code, and comprehensive monitoring, which are noted as necessary next steps.
key_questions_answered: What is the proposed architecture style and the rationale behind it?
What is the chosen technology stack and why was it selected over alternatives?
How does the architecture plan to support scalability and future feature development?
What are the major technical risks and dependencies?

anticipated_objections.objection: A microservices architecture is premature optimization and will introduce significant complexity and slow down the initial MVP development.
anticipated_objections.response: The concern about initial velocity is valid. However, the core product domains—inventory, payments, and sales analytics—are naturally decoupled. Starting with a services-oriented approach prevents building a tightly-coupled monolith that will be difficult to refactor later. We will mitigate the complexity by using managed cloud services (e.g., serverless functions or managed container orchestration) to reduce operational burden.

anticipated_objections.objection: React Native can introduce performance limitations and abstraction issues not present in native development.
anticipated_objections.response: We acknowledge the trade-offs. For this application, which is primarily forms-based data entry and display, the performance of React Native is more than sufficient. The significant advantage is the ability to maintain a single codebase for both iOS and Android, which is critical for a small engineering team and enables faster delivery of features to our entire user base.

anticipated_objections.objection: The plan lacks specifics on data persistence, inter-service communication, and API gateway strategy.
anticipated_objections.response: This is correct. This document presents the high-level architectural style. The next phase of design work will produce detailed diagrams for data models, select a message bus or event streaming platform for asynchronous communication, and define the API gateway patterns for security and routing. These are critical design decisions that will be made before implementation.

views.decision_recommendation: Recommend approval of the high-level architectural direction. Mandate a follow-up review after a prototyping phase to assess a more detailed design, including infrastructure choices, CI/CD strategy, and a proof-of-concept demonstrating the viability of the microservices pattern for the core team.

views.tailored_summary:
This initiative is grounded in clear, high-severity pain points for a specific, underserved user persona: the 'Tech-Hesitant Traditionalist' farmer's market vendor. Our research indicates significant frustration with manual inventory management for perishable goods and lost sales due to an inability to accept diverse payment types, especially SNAP/EBT. This provides a strong foundation for product-market fit.

Our key competitive differentiator against incumbents like Square is our niche focus. While Square offers a generic POS, we will provide a purpose-built solution with features tailored to this market, such as simplified perishable inventory tracking and integrated SNAP/EBT processing. The product roadmap is logically phased, starting with an MVP focused on the most critical user stories in inventory and payments ('EPIC-001', 'EPIC-002') to deliver immediate value and validate our core hypothesis.
key_questions_answered: What specific customer problem are we solving, and what is the evidence for it?
How will our product differentiate from established competitors like Square?
Who is our primary user persona and what are their core 'jobs to be done'?
What is the scope of the Minimum Viable Product (MVP)?

anticipated_objections.objection: The market seems small, and Square is a dominant player. Is there really room for a new solution?
anticipated_objections.response: Square's strength is its breadth, which is also its weakness. They are a general-purpose tool. Our strategy is to win by being the best solution for a specific vertical. By focusing deeply on the unique needs of farmers market vendors, like SNAP/EBT and perishable inventory, we create a value proposition that Square cannot easily match without diluting its core offering.

anticipated_objections.objection: Our primary persona is 'Tech-Hesitant.' This presents a significant adoption risk.
anticipated_objections.response: This is the central product and design challenge. It mandates a relentless focus on simplicity and an intuitive user experience. The freemium model is designed to lower the barrier to trial, and our GTM strategy of partnering with trusted market associations will help overcome initial skepticism. Onboarding and customer support must be exceptionally user-friendly.

anticipated_objections.objection: The evidence for these 'pain signals' is tiered as E3 and E4. How confident are we that these are the right problems to solve?
anticipated_objections.response: The evidence is based on industry knowledge and well-formed hypotheses, but it needs direct validation. This is a primary goal of our beachhead market launch. We will conduct direct customer interviews and usability tests with Bay Area vendors before and during the MVP rollout to confirm these pain points and ensure our feature prioritization is correct.

views.decision_recommendation: Strongly recommend proceeding to the product development phase. Prioritize building the MVP as defined by the 'Inventory Management' and 'Payment Processing' epics. Simultaneously, fund and execute a customer validation study in the beachhead market to refine UX and confirm feature prioritization.

common_concerns: The overall evidence score is low (0.29), with a heavy reliance on hypotheses (E4) and assumptions (E5) for critical financial, market, and technical claims. This indicates a high degree of uncertainty that must be addressed through validation.
The initial team size is very lean (2 Engineers, 1 PM, 0.5 Support), which poses a significant execution risk across product development, security, and go-to-market activities.
Competition from established, well-funded players like Square represents a persistent market risk that requires sharp and sustained product differentiation to overcome.
alignment_opportunities: All stakeholders can align around the core thesis that a niche, purpose-built solution can win against a generic horizontal competitor by super-serving a specific user's needs (e.g., SNAP/EBT processing).

There is a shared understanding that the 'Tech-Hesitant' nature of the user persona makes simplicity and ease-of-use a critical requirement that must inform product design, technical architecture, and financial modeling (e.g., support costs).

Agreement exists that the initial go-to-market phase in a 'beachhead' market is not just for revenue generation but is a critical exercise in validating the core assumptions of the entire business case.

experiments.target_profile: Farmers market vendors who have been operating for at least 2 seasons and currently use a mix of cash and at least one other payment method (e.g., Square, Venmo).
experiments.specific_instructions: 1. Prepare a semi-structured interview script focusing on current processes. 2. Ask open-ended questions about how they track sales, manage inventory (especially perishables), and handle payments. 3. Use the '5 Whys' technique to dig into pain points. 4. Do not mention our solution until the very end, if at all. 5. Record and transcribe interviews for analysis.
experiments.success_criteria: At least 8/12 vendors describe significant, unprompted pain related to inventory management or sales reconciliation that takes them more than 30 minutes per market day.
experiments.failure_criteria: Fewer than 4/12 vendors can articulate a significant problem, or most are happy with their current pen-and-paper or Square-based system.
experiments.risk_if_skipped: Building a solution for a problem that doesn't exist or isn't painful enough for vendors to pay to solve, leading to product failure.

experiments.target_profile: Farmers, growers, and makers who sell at community farmers markets in the US.
experiments.specific_instructions: 1. Create a simple landing page with a clear value proposition (e.g., 'The All-in-One POS for Farmers Markets. Sell more, waste less.'). 2. Include key hypothetical features (Perishable Inventory, EBT support, Sales Analytics). 3. Have a single call-to-action: 'Join the Waitlist for Early Access'. 4. Set up an ad campaign with a budget of $500 and track conversion rates and cost-per-email-signup.
experiments.success_criteria: Achieve a waitlist signup conversion rate of >5% and a cost-per-lead of <$15.
experiments.failure_criteria: Conversion rate is <2% or cost-per-lead is >$30, suggesting the channel is too expensive or the message is wrong.
experiments.risk_if_skipped: Inability to acquire customers at a cost-effective rate, making the entire business model unsustainable (LTV/CAC < 3).

experiments.target_profile: Farmers market vendors sourced from waitlist signups (from EXP-2) and targeted outreach.
experiments.specific_instructions: 1. Design a 5-7 minute online survey. 2. Briefly describe the product concept. 3. Use the Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter to ask about price points (too cheap, bargain, expensive, too expensive). 4. Ask respondents to rank the importance of key features (inventory, EBT, analytics, etc.).
experiments.success_criteria: The optimal price point from the Van Westendorp analysis falls between $35-$65/month, and at least 60% of respondents rank 'perishable inventory management' as a top 3 feature.
experiments.failure_criteria: The optimal price point is below $20/month, which would make the LTV calculation in FM-10 highly unlikely to be met.
experiments.risk_if_skipped: Mispricing the product, leading to either low adoption (if too high) or unsustainable unit economics (if too low).

experiments.target_profile: Vendors who participated in EXP-1 and expressed strong interest, or new recruits from local markets.
experiments.specific_instructions: 1. Create a clickable prototype (e.g., in Figma or InVision) of the 3 core workflows: adding a new product, processing a sale with mixed items, and viewing an end-of-day report. 2. Give users specific tasks to complete (e.g., 'Imagine a customer wants to buy 2 lbs of tomatoes and a bunch of carrots. Show me how you would ring that up.'). 3. Observe where they struggle or get confused without leading them. 4. Ask for their overall impression and if this would be an improvement over their current method.
experiments.success_criteria: At least 6/8 users can complete all core tasks, and 7/8 agree that the prototype represents a significant improvement over their current process.
experiments.failure_criteria: More than half the users are unable to complete a core task, or they express that it seems more complicated than their current system.
experiments.risk_if_skipped: Building an unusable or confusing product that fails to deliver on the value proposition, leading to high churn and negative word-of-mouth.

experiments.target_profile: 3-5 highly engaged vendors from the waitlist or interviews who are willing to be beta testers.
experiments.specific_instructions: 1. Set up a basic system using off-the-shelf tools (e.g., Google Sheets for inventory, Square for payments, WhatsApp for communication). 2. Manually manage their inventory and sales data for them for 2-4 market days. 3. At the end of the trial period, ask them to pay the target subscription price ($49) to continue the service. 4. The key is to validate if they will PAY for the value delivered, even when it's manual on the backend.
experiments.success_criteria: At least 2/3 of participating vendors convert to paying customers at the target price point after the trial.
experiments.failure_criteria: No vendors are willing to pay for the service after the trial, indicating a fundamental value proposition failure.
experiments.risk_if_skipped: Scaling a product that people like but are ultimately not willing to pay for, resulting in a failed business despite having users.
